subsystems.name: Collecting aperture
subsystems.role: a large dish or array that gathers faint radio waves; bigger dishes see weaker transmitters further away.

subsystems.name: Wideband digitising spectrometer
subsystems.role: splits gigahertz of bandwidth into hundreds of millions of very fine frequency channels.

subsystems.name: Search software
subsystems.role: finds signals that look artificial — extremely narrow in frequency and drifting slowly as the transmitter's planet moves.

subsystems.name: Interference rejection
subsystems.role: Earth's own transmitters are millions of times louder than any plausible beacon, so most effort goes into removing them.

subsystems.name: Optical and near-infrared channel
subsystems.role: looks for brief laser pulses using fast photometers and spectrographs.

subsystems.name: Archive and compute
subsystems.role: stores raw voltages and reduced spectra so future algorithms can re-examine old observations.

buildSteps.title: Pick targets
buildSteps.detail: Surveys choose nearby stars, known exoplanet hosts, the galactic centre and plane, or entire other galaxies, trading depth against sky coverage.

buildSteps.title: Instrument the telescope
buildSteps.detail: Wideband receivers and fast digitisers are fitted, often so the search runs alongside conventional astronomy without stealing observing time.

buildSteps.title: Observe and channelise
buildSteps.detail: The telescope tracks a target while the spectrometer slices the band into very narrow channels, typically hertz-wide.

buildSteps.title: Excise interference
buildSteps.detail: Signals seen when pointing away from the target, or by a second telescope, are flagged as human-made and removed.

buildSteps.title: Search for artificial structure
buildSteps.detail: Software looks for narrowband peaks that shift in frequency at a steady rate, as a beacon on a rotating, orbiting planet would.

buildSteps.title: Follow up candidates
buildSteps.detail: Any hit is re-observed on the same telescope and then on a different one to check it repeats from the same direction.

buildSteps.title: Verify or reject
buildSteps.detail: A signal must appear in independent instruments, survive interference tests and be announced openly; a 2019 candidate toward Proxima Centauri was traced to interference from equipment on Earth.

buildSteps.title: Archive and re-mine
buildSteps.detail: Data are kept so improved algorithms can search the same sky again.

prerequisites.tech: Radio astronomy with wideband digital receivers
prerequisites.why: the survey is only as good as the telescopes and spectrometers behind it.

prerequisites.tech: Cheap petabyte-scale storage and GPU compute
prerequisites.why: searches generate data far faster than humans can inspect them.
terrestrial and satellite transmissions increasingly drown weak cosmic signals.
a nanosecond laser pulse needs detectors fast enough to catch it.
industrial gases such as nitrogen dioxide or CFCs could reveal technology without any deliberate signal.

pathway.milestone: large dedicated surveys such as Breakthrough Listen on dishes including Green Bank, MeerKAT, FAST and Parkes, plus optical searches
pathway.unlocks: orders of magnitude more stars and frequencies examined than early searches.

pathway.milestone: next-generation arrays such as the Square Kilometre Array
pathway.unlocks: huge sensitivity and sky coverage, making commensal technosignature search routine.

pathway.milestone: coordinated multi-wavelength follow-up and atmospheric technosignature spectroscopy
pathway.unlocks: detection routes that do not depend on anyone deliberately broadcasting at us.

pathway.milestone: a verified detection confirmed by independent observatories
pathway.unlocks: the single most consequential result in the history of science — or, at minimum, far tighter limits on how alone we are.
